title: Extraction and characterization of biocompatible hydroxyapatite (Hap) from red big eye fish bone Potential for biomedica

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/Discussion, SEM paragraph ("Fig. 1 shows natural bone...")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The same paragraph states both "Fig. 2 displays nanoparticles from alkaline hydrolysis of the HAp" / "raw bone formed ... nanostructured particles when alkaline hydrolysed" AND "Based on the results, alkaline hydrolysis HAps do not contain nanoparticles." These statements are mutually exclusive; one of them must be wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, "Alkaline hydrolysis produces HAp that is purer and has larger crystals than thermal calcination."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This contradicts the preceding text: "Despite having larger particles than alkaline hydrolysis, thermal calcination eliminated the organic portion" and "HAp obtained at a lower temperature had larger surface area nanocrystals than HAp produced by the thermal calcination process at a higher temperature". The paper claims alkaline hydrolysis yields nanoparticles and thermal calcination yields agglomerated microstructures, so alkaline hydrolysis cannot also give the larger crystals.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("FESEM revealed spherical HAp particles with sizes ranging from 50 to 80 nm") vs. SEM results paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No particle size measurement, size distribution or spherical morphology is reported anywhere in the SEM results, which only state qualitatively that "HAp microcrystals longer than a few micrometres are seen in bone" and that "Alkaline hydrolysis maintains crystal size". If the crystal size of the micrometre-scale bone crystals is maintained, a 50–80 nm product is inconsistent; the abstract value is unsupported by the presented data.

The text states "Fig. 5(a)–(c) illustrate XRD reflections obtained from bone samples subjected to alkaline treatment, thermal calcination, and untreated red big eye bone", whereas the figure caption states "Fig. 5 (a–c) show XRD reflections of raw red big eye bone, treated bone, and thermal-calcinated bone." The panel assignments conflict, so the reader cannot know which trace corresponds to which sample.

predicted_errors.error_location: FTIR results, "These findings align with referenced spectra reported in literature [11,12]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: References [11] and [12] are introduced in the Introduction as sources on "applications of treated fish waste" and "adverse ecological impacts of fishery discards and the need for sustainable management", not on FT-IR spectra of hydroxyapatite. The citation cannot support the spectral band assignments claimed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, "Since the thermal calcination method was also used to separate HAp from chicken femur, sheep femur ... there is no degradation at a high temperature (1100 C) [21]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [21] is cited in the Introduction specifically for alkaline hydrolysis ("One such approach is alkaline hydrolysis, which offers several advantages ... [21]"). The same reference is here used for thermal calcination of chicken/sheep/bovine bone at 1100 °C — inconsistent attribution.

[28,29] are first cited as the origin of the alkaline hydrolysis route ("To prevent grinding, researchers created the alkaline hydrolysis approach for isolating nanostructured HAp from bovine bone [28,29]") and then, in the next paragraph, for the opposite claim ("the nanostructured HAp was obtained using a milling method [28,29]"). The same sources cannot support both contradictory statements.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, "...this work recovered that red giant eye bone, a novel marine source of nanostructured HAp [34]" and "We found that raw bone formed microstructure HAp ... [34]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The authors' own novel findings are attributed to an external reference [34]. Either the finding is not novel (contradicting the novelty claim) or the citation is misapplied.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1 Preparation (alkaline hydrolysis) and Discussion repeat of conditions
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The procedure describes treating bone powder in aqueous 2 M NaOH "at 250 °C for 5 h" in an open/unspecified vessel, followed by filtration. An aqueous alkaline solution cannot be held at 250 °C at atmospheric pressure (water boils at ~100 °C); a hydrothermal autoclave would be required but none is specified, making the stated method as written unworkable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion of thermal calcination, "CO₂, CaO, and (CO₃)₂ were kept at a high temperature of 1000 C, whereas dioxygen, calcium oxide, and carbonate ions were eliminated from fishbone...[27]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sentence is chemically incoherent and self-contradictory: the same species (CO₂/CaO/carbonate) are said to be both retained and eliminated; "(CO₃)₂" is not a valid chemical formula; and CO₂ is mis-equated with "dioxygen".

predicted_errors.error_location: FTIR results bullet list and following paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 566 cm⁻¹ (and 603 cm⁻¹) bands are ν4 O–P–O bending modes, not "phosphate stretching", and the paper assigns the 1455/1417/875 cm⁻¹ bands to HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) rather than carbonate (CO₃²⁻). Moreover, the presence of these carbonate bands contradicts the conclusion of "the generation of pure hydroxyapatite" and the abstract claim of "high-purity HAp".

predicted_errors.error_location: Characterization section, "SEM (JEOL JSM-5610LV Field Emission Gun)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The JEOL JSM-5610LV is a conventional tungsten-filament low-vacuum SEM, not a field-emission gun instrument; the abstract nonetheless reports "field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM)" and nanoscale (50–80 nm) measurements, which this instrument specification does not support.

predicted_errors.error_location: XRD results, "Analysis of surface area, crucial for understanding crystal size, often relies on X-ray diffraction (XRD) techniques"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: XRD peak broadening (Debye–Scherrer) yields crystallite size, not surface area; surface area requires methods such as BET. The stated rationale for the analysis is incorrect, and no Scherrer-derived crystallite sizes are actually reported.

predicted_errors.error_location: XRD results, "Schwertmann and Latham (1986) established that peak broadening in XRD spectra serves as a reliable parameter..."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A name–year citation appears in an otherwise numbered reference system, and no corresponding entry is traceable; attributing establishment of the XRD peak-broadening/crystallite-size relationship (Scherrer, 1918) to Schwertmann and Latham is a misattribution.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, "The cost-effective and environmentally friendly process further underscores the feasibility of scaling up this method for industrial applications"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No cost analysis, energy balance, life-cycle assessment, or scale-up experiment is presented anywhere in the paper; the claim of cost-effectiveness and industrial scalability is unsupported by the reported evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, "proliferation rate of 92 % compared to the control" / "Cytotoxicity tests indicated no significant adverse effects"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A single proliferation value is reported without indicating which material (A-HAp or T-HAp) or dose (12.5 vs 25 µg mL⁻¹) it refers to, without replicates, error estimates, or any statistical test, yet the word "significant" is used. Furthermore, 92 % of control represents a slight decrease in viability, which is presented as proof of biocompatibility without supporting analysis.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, "hydroxyapatite (Ca/P = 1.667) and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP, Ca/P = 1.5) being among the most extensively studied compounds [4]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [4] is used earlier in the same Introduction to support fish-waste production statistics in India; it is implausible that the same source supplies calcium phosphate ceramic Ca/P data, indicating a misapplied citation.
